bib.title: Learning to Continually Learn via Meta-learning Agentic Memory Designs

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Learning to Continually Learn via Meta-learning Agentic Memory Designs" (ALMA), Yiming Xiong, Shengran Hu, Jeff Clune (UBC, Vector Institute, CIFAR). arXiv 2602.07755v1, 8 Feb 2026, marked "Preprint. February 10, 2026". Code: github.com/zksha/alma.

COVERAGE: 200,809 chars extracted over 71 pages. I read all of the body (pp.1-9), all of Appendix A (algorithm, prompts header, pseudocode), B (benchmarks, baselines, learning and testing setup), and C.1-C.2 including Table 2. I skimmed the reference list (pp.9-15), the remaining Meta Agent prompt text, the per-benchmark prompt and response examples (Figs 7-10), and the example learned-code listing in C.3 (pp.39-71). Those are code and prompt dumps with no further results. Figures 11-13 (learning curves for TextWorld, ALFWorld, MiniHack) are image-only; only the archive-tree node scores came through. Page refs below are paper page numbers.

CLAIMS (ranked)
1. Meta-learned memory designs beat four hand-built designs on all four benchmarks, with the weaker agent.
 number: overall avg 12.3% vs 6.1% no-memory (+6.2). Best human baseline 8.6 (Trajectory Retrieval, +2.5). Others: Reasoning Bank 7.5, Dynamic Cheatsheet 7.2, G-Memory 7.7.
 setup: GPT-5-nano agent; Meta Agent GPT-5; designs learned and tested on the same FM. Static mode, mean±SE over 3 Deployment runs. ALFWorld, TextWorld, Baba Is AI, MiniHack.
 quote: "the learned memory designs achieve an overall improvement of 6.2% compared to the no-memory baseline, and outperform all state-of-the-art human-designed memory baselines."
 where: p.6, Table 1
2. The same designs transfer to a stronger agent (GPT-5-mini) without re-learning.
 number: ALMA 53.9% overall vs 41.1 no-memory (+12.8). Baselines: Trajectory Retrieval 48.6 (+7.5), Dynamic Cheatsheet 46.5 (+5.4), G-Memory 46.0 (+4.9), Reasoning Bank 40.1 (-1.0). Per benchmark ALMA: ALFWorld 87.1±1.4, TextWorld 75.0±2.3, Baba Is AI 33.3±2.4, MiniHack 20.0±2.9.
 setup: designs learned with GPT-5-nano, tested with GPT-5-mini in the agent, static mode.
 quote: "The learned memory designs improve the overall average success rate by 12.8% over the no-memory baseline and outperform all human-designed baselines."
 where: p.6, Table 1 bottom
3. Several human designs do nothing or hurt in some domains. This is the strongest "hand-built memory is not free" evidence.
 number: GPT-5-nano TextWorld: Trajectory Retrieval 2.7 (-2.7), G-Memory 2.1 (-3.3), Dynamic Cheatsheet 4.3 (-1.1) vs no-memory 5.4. GPT-5-mini: Reasoning Bank 67.1 vs 67.6 on ALFWorld, and MiniHack Dynamic Cheatsheet 11.7 (-3.3) vs 15.0.
 setup: as claims 1-2.
 quote: "Trajectory Retrieval5.2±1.9+2.32.7±0.9-2.719.0±6.3+9.57.5±1.4+0.88.6+2.5" (Table 1 row, raw extraction)
 where: p.6, Table 1
4. Open-ended archive search beats greedy search on ALFWorld.
 number: GPT-5-nano 12.4±0.5 vs greedy 11.9±0.5; GPT-5-mini 87.1±1.4 vs 77.1±0.8.
 setup: ALFWorld only, same budget of 43 designs; greedy always expands the current best design. Single ablation, one benchmark.
 quote: "(for GPT-5-nano, 11.9% vs 12.4%; for GPT-5-mini, 77.1% vs 87.1%), success rates are lower than those achieved by designs learned with open-ended exploration"
 where: p.6; Table 2, p.39
5. Learned memory scales with collected experience and adapts under distribution shift.
 number: 84.1% on ALFWorld valid unseen in dynamic mode. Fig 4 shows no numbers in text (a plot of 0-70 collection tasks).
 setup: GPT-5-mini; memory collected on 70 valid-seen tasks, deployed on valid-unseen (134 tasks) with memory updated after each task.
 quote: "the learned memory design achieves a success rate of 84.1% on ALFWorld, outperforming all human-designed baselines"
 where: p.7, Fig 4 and Fig 5. The paper notes more data is not monotonic: "increasing the trajectory size does not necessarily lead to a monotonic improvement in success rate".
6. Learned memory is cheaper than most baselines.
 number: end-to-end memory cost $0.09 across all benchmarks. Retrieved-context size: ALMA 1,319 tokens; Trajectory Retrieval 9,149; G-Memory 6,095; Dynamic Cheatsheet 2,258; Reasoning Bank 240 (cheapest in tokens). Fig 6 x-axis runs to about $1.6 for the baselines.
 setup: cost counts GPT-4o-mini and text-embedding-3-small calls only, from raw logs to retrieved context, over both phases; the cost is not optimised by ALMA. Token counts use the GPT-5-mini tokenizer.
 quote: "lower overall end-to-end memory cost across all benchmarks ($0.09) and appropriate token sizes of retrieved content."
 where: p.7, Fig 6 (p.9)
7. Learned designs specialise by domain. For ALFWorld and TextWorld (explicit object goals) they store fine-grained facts: affordance graphs, spatial graphs, room layouts. For Baba Is AI and MiniHack (harder reasoning) they favour abstract strategy libraries and plan synthesis, plus risk and spatial sub-modules.
 number: none
 quote: "the memory designs favor domain-specific abstract strategy, including strategy libraries and plan synthesis."
 where: p.7, Fig 3
8. Stepping-stone effect. Intermediate designs with moderate scores (property validation, spatial object normalisation) did not help immediately but fed into the best Baba Is AI design once "stall-triggered strategy switch" was added.
 number: none
 where: p.6, Fig 2

METHOD (needed for the note)
- A memory design is a triplet M=(U,D,R): update process, storage structure, retrieval process (App A.2). It is code against two interfaces, general_update(recorder) and general_retrieve(recorder), composed of Sub_memo_layer sub-modules. Each has retrieve/update and an optional own database. Layers can chain, one's output feeding the next. This covers vector DBs, graph DBs and dictionary DBs.
- Two phases. Memory Collection runs the agent with no memory access, then updates the memory per trajectory. Deployment retrieves from the memory per task. It is static (memory frozen) or dynamic (memory keeps updating). Learning uses static mode only, to cut variance. Success rate is averaged over Gdeployment.
- Loop: Meta Agent (GPT-5) samples up to 5 designs from the archive, reads code, stratified interaction logs and score, writes an idea and plan, implements it in code, and trial-runs it. Up to 3 debug retries follow. It is then evaluated and archived. Setup: 11 learning steps, 43 designs.
- Sampling is as in DGM (Zhang 2025e). Score is sigmoid(f−f0) − α·log(1+visits); probability is a softmax of that. Values: α=0.5, T=0.5. Every design keeps non-zero probability. Archive stores code, score, a stratified log subset, and visit count.
- Splits: ALFWorld learning set is the first 30 train tasks. TextWorld and Baba Is AI are split evenly. MiniHack uses 30% to learn and 70% to test. ALFWorld valid-seen has 140 tasks, valid-unseen 134, with a 100-step limit. Tools offered to designs: GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4.1, text-embedding-3-small. Agent in learning: GPT-5-nano/low. Test transfer: GPT-5-mini/medium.
- Baselines (B.2): Trajectory Retrieval (top-1 by task-description embedding cosine), ReasoningBank, Dynamic Cheatsheet cumulative (one global sheet), G-Memory (query, insight and interaction graphs; top-1 trajectory plus top-3 insights). All were run with GPT-4o-mini and text-embedding-3-small at test time for fairness.

LIMITS
- Authors concede: designs are learned offline on a fixed learning set, not online. Each candidate needs many rollouts, so online learning was too costly. Capability is bounded by the underlying FM, as the search is in code space. They do not demonstrate a system that learns both memory and the agent. Cost is not optimised (multi-objective search is future work). Safety: code runs in a sandbox with human review of the learned designs for harmful behaviour such as prompt injection. They call for systematic inspection at scale.
- Not shown, my reading and flagged as such: absolute rates are low in places. GPT-5-nano gets ALFWorld 12.4% and TextWorld 6.2%. Many gains on nano are within SE (for example the Baba Is AI tie of 19.0 for ALMA and Trajectory Retrieval). Only token-level memory is covered; parametric and latent memory are excluded. The best-of-43 design is picked by learning-set score. Greedy ablation, scaling (Fig 4) and distribution shift (Fig 5) are ALFWorld only. Only three Deployment runs. Everything uses OpenAI models. Test-set splits are by task, but benchmarks are game worlds, not conversational memory (the Mem0/Zep use case the intro cites), so conversational transfer is untested.
- Dated: the GPT-5-family models and the baseline versions are as of early 2026.

BUILDS ON: ADAS (Hu, Lu & Clune 2025) for Meta Agent and code search space; DGM (Zhang et al. 2025e) for archive sampling; AI-generating algorithms (Clune 2020); Go-Explore (Ecoffet et al. 2021) cited for sampling; novelty search and open-endedness (Lehman & Stanley 2008, 2011a,b); "Learning to continually learn" (Beaulieu et al. 2020); MAML (Finn 2017); NAS (Elsken 2019). Memory taxonomy from "Memory in the age of AI agents" (Hu et al. 2026). Baselines: G-Memory (Zhang 2025a), ReasoningBank (Ouyang 2025), Dynamic Cheatsheet (Suzgun 2025), Trajectory Retrieval (Park 2023; Xu 2024). Related memory designs: Mem0 (Chhikara 2025), Zep (Rasmussen 2025), Nemori (Nan 2025), Memp (Fang 2026). Concurrent: Zhang 2025d, which seeds from many hand-crafted designs and selects greedily. AgentSquare (Shang 2025) co-learns memory but evaluates only one-shot performance. Benchmarks: ALFWorld (Shridhar 2021), TextWorld (Côté 2019), Baba Is AI (Cloos 2025), MiniHack (Samvelyan 2021), BALROG (Paglieri 2025).

CODE (verbatim, App A.1, p.16)
```
class MemoStructure(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    async def general_retrieve(self, recorder: Basic_Recorder) -> Dict:
    @abstractmethod
    async def general_update(self, recorder: Basic_Recorder) -> None:
```
with Sub_memo_layer(ABC) having `database: Optional[Any]`, `async retrieve(**kwargs)`, `async update(**kwargs)`. The quotes are from the extraction, which mangled spacing.
Selection score (A.4, p.18): `J_i = f̂_Mi − α·log(1 + t_Mi)`, `f̂ = σ(λ(f_M − f0))`, p_i = softmax(J_i/T).
Pseudocode: Algorithm 1, p.23 (extraction lines 1877-1925).

FIGURES (captions via extraction; image-only content not inspected)
- Fig 1 (p.2): the ALMA loop. Sample from the archive, ideate and plan, implement, evaluate, store. Best single picture for the note.
- Fig 2 (p.7): Baba Is AI archive tree and learning curve, with stepping-stone mechanisms labelled. Shows why open-ended beats greedy.
- Fig 3 (p.7): the best learned design per domain, as sub-module and database diagrams (graph, embedding, dictionary DBs). Shows what "learned memory design" looks like.
- Fig 4 (p.8): ALFWorld success vs collection-task count (0-70), 5 designs. Fig 5 (p.8): ALFWorld distribution shift. Fig 6 (p.9): cost vs success bubble chart with token sizes. Table 1 (p.6) is the main result.
- Figs 11-14 (pp.37-38): per-benchmark learning curves and the greedy tree. Appendix only.

PROBLEMS: Extraction is clean text but figure/plot contents are lost (chart axes only). Table 1 cells are run together and the raw quote for them is ugly. The abstract's "git." is a stray fragment. grep on the file was flaky, so I located sections with Python. No embedded instructions found in the PDF. The extracted text is at /tmp/alma.txt.
